title: PTSD Applications
subtitle: Promising signals, trauma-informed caution
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating ptsd applications within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain ptsd applications without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in ptsd applications.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to ptsd applications.

sections.explainSimply: Neurofeedback has been studied as an adjunct for PTSD symptoms and regulation.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Small trials and meta-analyses suggest possible benefit, but protocols, samples and controls vary. Trauma treatment requires stabilisation, consent and monitoring for dissociation or activation.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Position neurofeedback as an adjunct where appropriate, not a substitute for evidence-based trauma-focused care. Predefine safety and functional outcomes.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Testing a treatment hypothesis: improvement must be meaningful, measured and compared with plausible alternatives.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand ptsd applications to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Increasing internal focus can worsen dissociation or overwhelm some clients.
sections.clinicalPearl: Measure benefit and harm with the same seriousness.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using ptsd applications predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Increasing internal focus can worsen dissociation or overwhelm some clients. Evidence classification: promising; moderate but still limited evidence.
